title: Atlas Math Olympiad: Proof Edition
provenance: These exercises were prepared for this programme using established mathematics. The collection makes no claim of first discovery or official contest provenance.
verification: The worked arguments support the general conclusions. The executable checks provide separate evidence for specified finite cases. The challenge bands are editorial judgements and have not been calibrated against human contest performance.

problems.title: The Last Counter
problems.subject: Invariants
problems.intro: Put eight counters on one bench. Spend two to send one to the next bench. Can you make seven trades? Can you predict exactly which positions are reachable on any ring?
statement: Arrange n benches in a clockwise ring, where n ≥ 2. A position lists a nonnegative integer number of counters at each bench. A trade at a bench removes two of its counters and puts one counter at the next bench. A bench needs at least two counters to trade. After the last bench comes the first.

Given any starting position x and proposed finishing position y on the same labelled ring, find a necessary and sufficient test for reaching y from x. Your test must use the two lists of numbers without searching through possible orders of trades. Prove both directions, including the case of an empty target. You may stop at any time or make zero trades.

checkpoints.prompt: Three benches A, B, C start at (8, 0, 0). What is the greatest number of trades you can make?
checkpoints.explanation: Trade four times at A, twice at B and once at C. One counter returns to A. Each trade reduces the total by one and leaves at least one counter, so seven is the maximum.

checkpoints.prompt: Four benches A, B, C, D start at (15, 0, 0, 0). Play until no trade is legal. How many counters remain?
checkpoints.explanation: Give counters at A, B, C and D weights 1, 2, 4 and 8. Trades at A, B and C preserve total weight. A first trade at D would need weight at least 16, but the total before it would still be 15. At the end each bench holds at most one counter, and all four weights are needed to make 15.

hints: A trade has a direction. How could multiplying the counts at successive benches by 1, 2, 4, 8, … make a trade invisible? What happens at the wrap from the last bench to the first?
Label the benches 0 through n − 1. Let f[i] count the trades at i. A bench spends twice its own trade count and receives the previous bench’s trade count. Try determining the last trade count first.
A list of nonnegative trade counts balances the books. You still have to prove the counters can be spent in a legal order. What happens if you run the proposed trades backwards, starting with y?

In reverse, trade i needs one counter at bench i + 1. If trade i is still owed but bench i + 1 is empty, what does the balance equation at i + 1 imply about the reverse trades still owed there? Follow that implication around the ring.

proof.title: Count the trades across the last edge
proof.body: Number the benches 0 through n − 1. Give a counter at bench i weight 2ⁱ and write W(z) for the sum of these weights in position z. A forward trade at any bench except the last preserves W. At the last bench it spends weight 2ⁿ and creates weight 1. Thus its trade count must be f[n − 1] = (W(x) − W(y))/(2ⁿ − 1).

proof.title: Recover a unique candidate
proof.body: Set f[n − 1] to that quotient. For i decreasing from n − 1 to 1, compute f[i − 1] = y[i] − x[i] + 2f[i]. These are the balance equations y[i] = x[i] − 2f[i] + f[i − 1]. The equation for bench 0 also holds, with f[−1] interpreted as f[n − 1]. Indeed, the predicted final position from these counts has weight W(x) − (2ⁿ − 1)f[n − 1] = W(y). It already agrees with y on benches 1 through n − 1, so it agrees on bench 0 as well.

proof.title: State the test
proof.body: An empty target is reachable exactly when the start is empty. Every actual trade puts a counter on the next bench. For a nonempty target, accept exactly when every candidate f[i] is a nonnegative integer. Any legal play has these counts by the preceding equations, proving necessity.

proof.title: Construct a legal order backwards
proof.body: Start at z = y with r[i] = f[i] reverse trades still owed at each bench. A reverse trade of type i takes one counter from bench i + 1 and puts two at i. Perform any owed reverse trade whose source holds a counter, then decrease its r[i] by one. Throughout, x[j] = z[j] + 2r[j] − r[j − 1], with indices read around the ring. If some r[i] > 0 and no owed trade is legal, then z[i + 1] = 0. Applying the equation at i + 1 gives 2r[i + 1] = x[i + 1] + r[i] > 0. The same reasoning goes all the way around the ring. Every reverse type is owed and every bench is empty. Yet y began nonempty and each reverse trade increases the total by one. This contradiction guarantees a legal move until all debts vanish. The equations then give z = x. Read the moves in reverse order to obtain legal forward play from x to y.

rubric: Choose weights that identify the exact number of trades from the last bench to the first.
Derive all remaining trade counts, justify the equation at the first bench and test for nonnegative integers.
Settle the empty target separately and prove that any accepted nonempty target has a legal sequence of trades.

transfer.prompt: Change the price to three counters for one at the next bench. On a four-bench ring A, B, C, D, start with counters only at A. Finish with exactly two at B and one at D. Every bench must have traded at least once. What is the smallest possible starting pile?
transfer.explanation: Use weights 1, 3, 9 and 27. The target weighs 33. A trade at D decreases weight by 80, and trades elsewhere preserve it. At least one trade at D forces a starting pile of at least 113. From 113, trade 37 times at A, 12 at B, 4 at C, once at D and once more at A. The successive positions are (2, 37, 0, 0), (2, 1, 12, 0), (2, 1, 0, 4), (3, 1, 0, 1) and (0, 2, 0, 1).

problems.title: The shifted squares
problems.subject: Algebra
problems.intro: Two machines square an integer. One also adds a fixed shift. Which polynomials can divide their own outputs from both machines?
statement: Choose a nonzero integer c and a nonconstant monic polynomial P with integer coefficients. Monic means that its leading coefficient is 1. For every positive integer n with P(n) ≠ 0, require P(n) to divide both P(n²) and P(n² + c).

Determine every possible pair (c, P). Prove that your list is complete and that every member passes both tests. As an extension, decide whether the list changes if both tests need to hold for only infinitely many positive integers n.
You may use the fundamental theorem of algebra in the form that a degree-d complex polynomial has d roots when multiplicities are counted.

checkpoints.prompt: A nonzero root returns to an earlier value after repeated squaring. What must its absolute value be?
checkpoints.explanation: Some iterates satisfy z^(2ʲ) = z^(2ᵏ) with j < k. Dividing gives a positive power of z equal to 1.

checkpoints.prompt: Every root and both of its images lie in the closed unit disk. What is the largest possible absolute value of the shift c?
checkpoints.explanation: The points z² and z² + c are at distance |c|. The unit disk has diameter 2, and c = −2 actually occurs for P(x) = x² − 1.

checkpoints.prompt: For c = −1, suppose P(x) = (x + 1)³(x − 1)⁴xᵈ. What is the greatest d for which the two tests hold?
checkpoints.explanation: At 0 the shifted map hits −1 to order 2, so d ≤ 2 × 3. The simple preimages at 1 and −1 require 3 ≤ 4 ≤ d. Thus d = 6 works.

hints: Divide P(x² + c) by P(x) as polynomials. How large can the remainder at n be compared with P(n) as n tends to infinity? Apply the same argument with shift zero.
After lifting the divisibility to polynomials, follow a complex root under repeated squaring. Both z² and z² + c must now belong to the set consisting of 0 and the unit circle.
When |c| = 1, find the intersection of two unit circles with centres one unit apart. A point in that intersection is only a candidate: both of its next images must still be allowed.
Keep a multiplicity on each surviving root. Usually composition preserves the multiplicity of its image. At the input 0, the maps x² and x² + c double it.

proof.title: Turn the integer tests into polynomial identities
proof.body: For f(x) = x² or x² + c, divide P(f(x)) by the monic P(x). The quotient and remainder R have integer coefficients, and R is zero or has smaller degree than P. At each tested n, the nonzero integer P(n) divides R(n). For all sufficiently large n, |R(n)| < |P(n)|. Thus R vanishes at infinitely many n and is identically zero. The converse follows by evaluating the integer-coefficient quotient. This already answers the extension: infinitely many simultaneous successes give the very same identities.

proof.title: Trap the roots
proof.body: Let S be the finite, nonempty set of complex roots of P. Divisibility forces both z² and z² + c into S whenever z is in S. Repeated squaring of any nonzero root must revisit an earlier value, so that root is a root of unity. Hence every root is either 0 or has absolute value 1. The distance between z² and z² + c is |c| ≤ 2. Only −2, −1, 1 and 2 remain.

proof.title: Multiplicity is the second test
proof.body: Write m(z) for the multiplicity of z in P. At a root z and for either map f, the multiplicity of z in P(f(x)) is m(f(z)) times the order of the zero of f(x) − f(z) at x = z. Since f(x) − f(z) = (x − z)(x + z), this factor is 1 if z ≠ 0 and 2 if z = 0. Consequently a root set closed under both maps gives divisibility precisely when m(z) is at most that product for every root and both maps. This criterion proves sufficiency as well as necessity, since it counts every linear factor of P.

proof.title: Shifts of size two
proof.body: Two points in the closed unit disk can be two units apart on a horizontal line only at the endpoints −1 and 1. For c = 2 we must have z² = −1 for every root z. But −1 is then itself a root and its shifted image is 3, impossible. For c = −2 we must have z² = 1, and its two images 1 and −1 both occur. Both roots are nonzero, and each maps to 1 by squaring and to −1 by shifted squaring. Their multiplicities must be equal. Exactly P(x) = (x² − 1)ᵏ, with k any positive integer, works.

proof.title: The negative unit shift
proof.body: For c = −1 let t = z². If t is neither 0 nor 1, both t and t − 1 have absolute value 1. Subtracting their squared absolute values gives Re(t) = 1/2, and then Re(t²) = −1/2. But t is itself a root, so t² − 1 must be a root, although |t² − 1|² = 3. Therefore z² is 0 or 1. The only roots are 0, −1 and 1, and all three occur because 0 goes to −1, −1 goes to 1, and 1 goes to 0 under appropriate maps. Put a = m(−1), b = m(1), d = m(0). At −1 and 1 the images are 1 and 0. At 0 they are 0 and −1, each reached to order 2. The full criterion reduces to a ≤ b ≤ d ≤ 2a. All polynomials P(x) = (x + 1)ᵃ(x − 1)ᵇxᵈ with positive integers satisfying these inequalities work.

proof.title: The positive unit shift
proof.body: For c = 1, zero cannot occur: its shifted image is 1 and the shifted image of 1 is 2. For any root z, t = z² and t + 1 now both have absolute value 1, giving Re(t) = −1/2. Thus t is one of the two nonreal cube roots of unity, say ω and ω². The four possible z are ω, ω², −ω and −ω². They are exactly the roots of x⁴ + x² + 1. From any one of them, squaring reaches one of ω and ω², which squaring interchanges. Shifted squaring from these two reaches the other pair, using 1 + ω = −ω² and 1 + ω² = −ω. Hence each candidate reaches every other, and the four-point set is closed under both maps. Multiplicities cannot decrease along these steps, so they all agree. Exactly P(x) = (x⁴ + x² + 1)ᵏ with k any positive integer works. Together with the two negative shifts this exhausts the list.

rubric: Justify the passage from divisibility at integers to divisibility in the polynomial ring, including the variant with infinitely many test values.
Prove the unit-circle obstruction, bound c, and check that candidate roots survive further iterations of both maps.
Track multiplicities at every surviving root, including the exceptional input 0, and obtain all three families with the correct exponent restrictions.
Verify that all listed polynomials pass both tests and that each excluded shift or root has a demonstrated obstruction.

transfer.prompt: How many different admissible pairs (c, P) have P of degree exactly 36?
transfer.explanation: For c = −1, write 36 = a + b + d with a ≤ b ≤ d ≤ 2a. Then 8 ≤ a ≤ 12 and max(a, 36 − 3a) ≤ b ≤ floor((36 − a)/2). The five values of a give 3, 5, 4, 2 and 1 choices, totalling 15. For c = −2 there is one power of the quadratic, and for c = 1 one power of the quartic. The total is 17.

problems.credit: Designed for the Atlas Math Olympiad. Techniques include polynomial division, finite root orbits and multiplicity under composition.

problems.title: The Three-Turn Triangle
problems.subject: Geometry
problems.intro: Move three side midpoints at right angles to their sides. Can a third move restore the shape of every starting triangle?
statement: Start with any labelled, noncollinear triangle ABC in the plane. A pass has a real setting s. To construct A′, start at the midpoint of BC, turn the arrow from B to C anticlockwise through 90°, multiply that arrow by s, and add it to the midpoint. Construct B′ from the arrow from C to A and C′ from the arrow from A to B in the same way. A negative setting reverses the turned arrow. Keep these cyclic labels on every pass, even if the orientation changes. A zero-length arrow contributes zero displacement.

Use settings 1/2, 1/6 and t in that order, always working on the latest triple. Let G be the centroid of the original triangle. Prove that every pass preserves G. Find the unique real t for which, for every starting triangle, the three final arrows from G are all the same scalar multiple r of their corresponding original arrows from G. Determine r and prove the uniqueness of t.

Now replace the first two settings by any real numbers a and b. Determine exactly when there is one possible third setting, when there is none, and when every third setting works. Allow r = 0 in this classification, meaning that all three final vertices coincide at G.
problems.diagramAlt: First pass at setting one half. A is at (0,0), B at (8,0) and C at (0,4). From the midpoint M at (4,2), a perpendicular arrow ends at A′ at (2,−2). The arrow on BC points from B towards C.

checkpoints.prompt: In the illustrated triangle let A = (0,0), B = (8,0), C = (0,4). Reverse the pictured setting to s = −1/2. What is the new y-coordinate of A′?
checkpoints.explanation: The arrow from B to C is (−8,4). Its anticlockwise quarter-turn is (−4,−8). Subtract half of that vector from the midpoint (4,2) to reach (6,6).

checkpoints.prompt: Write J for the anticlockwise quarter-turn. For vectors u + v + w = 0 define K(u,v,w) = (J(w−v), J(u−w), J(v−u)). Applying K twice gives m times the original triple. What integer is m?
checkpoints.explanation: The first component after two applications is J(J(v−u) − J(u−w)) = −v + 2u − w = 3u. Cycling the letters gives the other two components.

checkpoints.prompt: Use the setting that works after 1/2 and 1/6. If the original distance GA is 60 units, how far is the final vertex with label A from G?
checkpoints.explanation: The three passes scale each position vector from G by 1/12, so a distance of 60 becomes 5.

hints: The three directed side arrows form a closed walk. Add the three midpoint positions and then add the three perpendicular displacements.

Work from G as origin. If u, v and w are the vertex vectors, their sum vanishes. The midpoint opposite u therefore has vector −u/2. Use K from the second checkpoint to write one whole pass as a single operation.
Once K² is known, two passes act as a multiple of the identity plus a multiple of K. Multiply by the third pass and look for the coefficient of K.

For necessity, try the illustrated right triangle. Its arrow from G to A is parallel to (2,1), while the perpendicular to BC is parallel to (1,2). A nonzero multiple of the second direction cannot be absorbed into a multiple of the first.

proof.title: Follow the centroid
proof.body: Write J for the anticlockwise quarter-turn of a vector, so J is linear and J² sends x to −x. The three side midpoints sum, as position vectors, to A + B + C. The sum of the three added arrows is sJ((C−B) + (A−C) + (B−A)) = 0. The average of the new positions is therefore G on every pass.

proof.title: Turn the side differences twice
proof.body: Place the origin at G and write X = (u,v,w) for the centred vertex vectors. Then u + v + w = 0. The midpoint opposite u is −u/2. With KX = (J(w−v), J(u−w), J(v−u)), a pass sends X to TₛX = (−I/2 + sK)X, where I leaves X fixed. The components of KX sum to zero, so the same formula applies again. The first component of K²X is J(J(v−u) − J(u−w)) = 2u − v − w = 3u. The other components are 3v and 3w by cyclic relabelling. Hence K² = 3I on centred triples.

proof.title: Find the third setting
proof.body: The passes with settings 1/2 and 1/6 together give (−I/2 + K/6)(−I/2 + K/2) = I/2 − K/3. After the third pass the operation is (−1/4 − t)I + (1/6 + t/2)K. Taking t = −1/3 cancels the K term. The coefficient of I becomes 1/12, so each final vertex lies one twelfth of the way from G to its original vertex.

proof.title: Prove that cancellation is necessary
proof.body: Use A = (0,0), B = (8,0), C = (0,4). Here G = (8/3,4/3), so u = (−8/3,−4/3), while the first component of KX is J(C−B) = (−4,−8). These two vectors are not parallel. If an operation αI + βK scales the arrows from G for every starting triangle, its first component on this example must be parallel to u or zero. This forces β = 0. In particular the setting −1/3 found above is unique.

proof.title: Classify all first and second settings
proof.body: For settings a and b, the first two passes give (1/4 + 3ab)I − ((a+b)/2)K. After setting t, the coefficient of K is (a+b + t(1+12ab))/4. The preceding triangle shows that it must vanish, and its vanishing is sufficient. If 1+12ab ≠ 0, the unique setting is t = −(a+b)/(1+12ab). If 1+12ab = 0 and a+b ≠ 0, there is no setting. If both are zero, every t works. In the last case the first two passes already give the zero operation, so every vertex has reached G before the third pass.

rubric: Show that the three added arrows sum to zero and that the three midpoint positions have the original centroid.
Represent a pass on centred vectors and prove the identity K² = 3I, or give a geometric argument with the same consequence.
Derive t = −1/3 and r = 1/12, and establish why no other third setting works for every triangle.
Give the full classification for arbitrary a and b, including both possibilities when 1+12ab vanishes.

transfer.prompt: A machine has first settings 1 and 2. Write its unique restoring setting as a reduced fraction with positive denominator. What is that denominator?
transfer.explanation: The equation is 3 + 25t = 0, so t = −3/25. Since 3 and 25 are coprime, the denominator is 25.

problems.title: The Two Missing Lamps
problems.subject: Combinatorics
problems.intro: An eight-lamp cube can tilt through many coordinates at once. How tightly must the lit lamps cluster to contain the most cubes?
statement: Let n ≥ k ≥ 4 be integers. Every binary string of length n represents a lamp. Add two strings coordinate by coordinate modulo 2. Exactly 2ᵏ − 2 of the lamps are lit, and S is their set.

An affine j-flat is a set of the form {a + ε₁v₁ + ⋯ + εⱼvⱼ : each εᵢ is 0 or 1}, where the 2ʲ choices give distinct points. An intact cube is an affine 3-flat with all eight lamps lit. Count each eight-point set once, whatever its base point or generating directions.
Determine the largest possible number of intact cubes as a function of k and n. Prove the bound, exhibit a configuration attaining it, and characterise every configuration attaining it.

checkpoints.prompt: Suppose 30 lamps are lit. What is the greatest possible number of nonzero directions v for which adding v pairs off all 30 lamps?
checkpoints.explanation: Two distinct nonzero periods u and v would partition S into four-point sets {x, x + u, x + v, x + u + v}. Four does not divide 30. Fifteen parallel pairs realise one period.

checkpoints.prompt: In a 16-point affine 4-flat, remove two points. How many four-point affine 2-flats survive?
checkpoints.explanation: There are 140 planes originally. Each deleted point lies in 35, and seven planes contain both. Inclusion–exclusion gives 140 − 70 + 7 = 77. The seven through both correspond to the seven nonzero directions after quotienting by the line joining the two points.

checkpoints.prompt: With n = 8 and k = 5, what is the maximum number of intact eight-point cubes?
checkpoints.explanation: For q = 32 the sharp formula gives (30 × 28 × 24 × 23) / 1344 = 345. Five dimensions suffice for the construction.

hints: Start with four lamps. A four-point plane is two disjoint pairs having the same difference v. In how many directions does a given plane get counted?

For a set B, the directions v satisfying B + v = B are its periods. If |B| is twice an odd number, ask how many nonzero periods can coexist. For an odd set with one lamp unpaired in direction v, sum all its points modulo 2 to locate the unpaired lamp.

For each nonzero v, identify x with x + v. Mark a quotient point only when both original lamps are lit. A cube whose direction space contains v projects to a four-point plane in these marked quotient points.

Write h = 2ᵏ / 2. Separate quotient sets of sizes h − 1 and h − 2. For all smaller sizes r, count triples to bound the number of planes per point. Finally sum over directions. Each original pair of lit lamps contributes to exactly one quotient size.

proof.title: The target and its local count
proof.body: Put q = 2ᵏ and h = q/2. The maximum is (q − 2)(q − 4)(q − 8)(q − 9)/1344. Its maximisers are exactly the affine k-flats with any two distinct points removed. To prove this, let P(B) count four-point planes in any binary point set B. For nonzero v let a(v) count unordered pairs {x, x + v} in B. Then ∑a(v) = C(|B|, 2), where C denotes a binomial coefficient. Two different pairs of difference v form a plane. Each plane has exactly three nonzero directions, so 3P(B) = ∑ C(a(v), 2). All sums over directions below exclude zero.

proof.title: A nearly full odd set
proof.body: Take |B| = h − 1 and put R = (h − 2)/2. At most R disjoint pairs can have any one difference. For 0 ≤ a ≤ R, C(a, 2) ≤ a(R − 1)/2, with equality only at 0 or R. The pair count gives P(B) ≤ (h − 1)(h − 2)(h − 4)/24. A flat of size h with one point removed attains this bound, since every direction within the flat leaves exactly one unpaired point.

proof.title: Recover the missing point from the odd set
proof.body: Suppose the odd-set bound is attained and let c be the sum of all points of B. In every direction v occurring as a difference there are R pairs and one unmatched point u. Each pair sums to v and R = h/2 − 1 is odd. Thus c = u + v. In particular c lies outside B, since otherwise u would have a partner. The set B ∪ {c} is now invariant under every occurring difference. Let W be their linear span and fix b in B. All points of B lie in b + W, and so does c = u + v. Conversely invariance under the generating differences puts every point of b + W in B ∪ {c}. This proves that equality forces a flat of size h with one point removed.

proof.title: The even set can have only one perfect pairing
proof.body: Now let |B| = r = h − 2 and R = r/2. A direction with a(v) = R translates all of B onto itself. Two such directions u and v would partition B into four-point planes parallel to {0, u, v, u + v}, impossible since r is 2 modulo 4. In every other direction a(v) ≤ R − 1, so C(a(v), 2) ≤ a(v)(R − 2)/2. The one possible perfect direction adds at most R/2 to this sum-bound. Hence 3P(B) ≤ (R − 2)C(r, 2)/2 + R/2, giving P(B) ≤ r(h − 4)(h − 5)/24. Remove two points x and y from a flat of size h. Their difference gives R pairs, every other direction in the flat gives R − 1, and outside directions give zero. This attains the bound.

proof.title: Price the planes in a quotient
proof.body: Put A = (h − 4)(h − 5)/24 and D = (h − 2)(h − 4)/24. For any r ≤ h − 3, three distinct points determine the unique four-point plane completed by their sum. Each plane contains four triples, so P(B) ≤ C(r, 3)/4 ≤ Ar. The last inequality follows from (r − 1)(r − 2) ≤ (h − 4)(h − 5) for r ≥ 3; smaller sets have no plane. The even-set bound extends P(B) ≤ Ar to r = h − 2. For r = h − 1 the odd-set bound is instead P(B) ≤ Dr, with D − A = (h − 4)/8 > 0.

proof.title: Count eight-point cubes through each direction
proof.body: For nonzero v, the quotient identifies each pair {x, x + v} as one point, with addition inherited from the original space. Let Bᵥ consist of quotient points with both lamps lit and put rᵥ = |Bᵥ|. A four-point plane in Bᵥ lifts to one eight-point cube, and every cube with v among its directions arises this way. Each cube has seven nonzero directions. Thus 7 times the cube count equals ∑P(Bᵥ). Also ∑rᵥ = C(2h − 2, 2). Each rᵥ is at most h − 1, and equality means v is a period of S. As |S| is 2 modulo 4, at most one v earns the larger rate D. Consequently 7 times the cube count is at most A C(2h − 2, 2) + (D − A)(h − 1). Expanding and dividing by seven gives the claimed formula.

proof.title: Attainment and rigidity
proof.body: Take a k-flat and delete x and y. In direction x + y its projected marked set is a flat of size h missing one point. In every other nonzero direction parallel to the k-flat the projected set is a flat of size h missing two points. In all remaining directions it is empty. Each bound used in the sum is attained. Conversely, equality requires the positive premium (D − A)(h − 1) and equality in its odd-set bound. Hence some period v pairs all of S, and Bᵥ is a flat of size h missing one point. The inverse image of that whole flat is a k-flat of size 2h. The sole missing quotient point lifts to a missing pair. All other lamps in this k-flat belong to S.

rubric: 1 point for the common-difference pair count for four-point planes and the sharp construction.
2 points for the odd-set plane bound and the equality proof that recovers the missing point.
2 points for the even-set bound, the single-period obstruction and the uniform bound for all smaller quotient sizes.
2 points for the seven-direction quotient count, the sharp maximum and the classification of every maximiser.

transfer.prompt: In the 64-point binary space of dimension 6, exactly 30 lamps are lit. How many distinct lighting patterns attain the maximum?
transfer.explanation: Each pattern occupies a unique affine 5-flat. Distinct 5-flats meet in at most 16 points, whereas the pattern contains 30. There are 63 nonzero binary linear functionals, each with two level sets, giving 126 affine 5-flats. Distinct nonzero functionals have distinct kernels over the binary field. Choose the two missing points in C(32, 2) = 496 ways. The product is 62,496.

problems.credit: Designed for the Atlas Math Olympiad. Related background on four-point planes appears in Marcus Brinkmann, Classification of Almost Perfect Nonlinear Functions up to Dimension Five (2007), Chapter 3.

investigations.last-counter: Let the price of a trade vary from bench to bench: on successive benches require 2, 3 and 2 counters to send one onwards. Find weights that stay unchanged at the first two benches. Enumerate small starting positions and look for a reachability test. Which part of your argument still works for an arbitrary cyclic list of integer prices at least two?
investigations.shifted-squares: Replace both squaring machines by cubing machines, with outputs P(n³) and P(n³ + c). Begin with monic linear polynomials and prove your complete list for that degree. Which restrictions on the roots survive in higher degree? Separate a proved restriction from a classification you have only tested.
investigations.three-turn-triangle: Keep the cyclic labels but replace the anticlockwise 90° turn in every pass by 60°. First test settings 1/2 and 1/6 on a non-equilateral triangle. Can any real third setting restore every labelled triangle up to a real scaling about its centroid? Explain whether a single test triangle can establish or refute your claim.
investigations.two-missing-lamps: Remove four points from a four-dimensional binary affine flat. Compare the intact cube counts when the four missing points form a plane and when they are affinely independent. Prove your counts by inclusion and exclusion or exhaustive enumeration, then ask which pattern you would predict for four missing points in higher dimension.

last-counter.title: Which ticket bundle can the club promise?
last-counter.scenario: A games club is trying a three-colour ticket exchange. Two red tickets buy one blue, two blue buy one gold, and two gold buy one red. A visitor has eight red tickets. The organiser wants to advertise one of two four-ticket bundles.
last-counter.question: Which bundle can the visitor obtain without borrowing tickets: two red, one blue and one gold, or two red and two blue? Predict whether either, both or neither is possible.
model: The first bundle is possible. Make three red exchanges to get two red and three blue. Exchange two of those blue for one gold. The visitor now has two red, one blue and one gold.

Give red, blue and gold tickets weights 1, 2 and 4. The first two exchanges preserve weight, and a gold exchange reduces weight by 7. The starting weight is 8. The second bundle weighs 6, a reduction of 2, so no legal exchange sequence can produce it.
last-counter.limitation: The conclusion depends on the club enforcing the three rates exactly. A free ticket, a reverse exchange or a loan changes which promises it can keep.
last-counter.investigate: Use three labelled cups and paper tickets. Start with eight red, record the counts after each trade, and check the weight after each step. Repeat from nine red and try to build the two advertised bundles again.

three-turn-triangle.title: Will a map icon fit its printed box?
three-turn-triangle.scenario: A designer builds a triangular map icon by applying the problem’s three midpoint passes. The original right triangle has horizontal and vertical legs of 120 mm and 90 mm. The finished icon must keep the same orientation and exactly fill a 10 mm by 7.5 mm box.
three-turn-triangle.question: After settings 1/2 and 1/6, which signed third setting should the designer use? Predict the final length of the sloping edge before measuring it.
model: Choose −1/3. The proof gives a scale of +1/12 about the original centroid. Every edge vector keeps its direction and becomes one twelfth as long. The legs become 10 mm and 7.5 mm, which gives the required bounding box.
The original sloping edge measures 150 mm by Pythagoras. Its predicted final length is 12.5 mm. The centroid also stays fixed, so it gives the designer a second check on placement.
three-turn-triangle.limitation: The dimensions describe the triangle’s vertex positions. A thick outline can extend beyond them, and rounding after each pass can move the final vertices.
three-turn-triangle.investigate: Draw the three passes on graph paper or in a drawing tool, retaining the cyclic labels. Measure the final three sides and the shift of the centroid. Repeat with a scalene triangle of your own and compare each measured ratio with 1/12.

shifted-squares.title: Can a logger regroup time bins without splitting one?
shifted-squares.scenario: A classroom sensor logger groups readings into bins that start from a common time zero. In integer mode n ≥ 2, each bin is P(n) = n² − 1 ticks wide. A proposed update changes the mode to n² or n² − 2. The designer wants every new bin to contain a whole number of complete old bins.
shifted-squares.question: At n = 3, predict how many old bins fit after each update. Would replacing the second update by n² + 2 also work for every mode?
model: An old bin is 8 ticks wide. The new modes 9 and 7 give widths 80 and 48, so one new bin holds 10 or 6 old bins. For any n ≥ 2 the two new widths factor as (n² − 1)(n² + 1) and (n² − 1)(n² − 3). Each ratio is a positive integer.
The proposed +2 update also passes at n = 3, but fails at n = 4. The old width is 15 and the new width is 18² − 1 = 323. A boundary at tick 323 cuts the old bin from tick 315 to tick 330.
shifted-squares.limitation: Divisibility settles boundary alignment for a shared time zero and exact integer ticks. It cannot recover readings missing from an old bin or align clocks with different starting offsets.
shifted-squares.investigate: In a spreadsheet, list n from 2 to 10. For each update divide the new width by the old and record the remainder. Then shift the new bin origin by one tick and mark its first boundary on a timeline to see which prediction depended on the shared origin.

two-missing-lamps.title: Which fourteen switch tests should the lab run?
two-missing-lamps.scenario: A prototype has five on/off switches A through E. The lab can run 14 of 32 settings. It wants complete eight-run experiments in which three independent toggle actions can each be on or off. An action may flip several switches together. Count each distinct eight-setting experiment once.
two-missing-lamps.question: Schedule I runs every setting with E off except 00000 and 11110, writing switches in ABCDE order. Schedule II replaces 00110 in that list with 00111. Which schedule preserves more complete experiments? Does the winner ever exercise switch E in its on position?
model: Schedule I attains the theorem’s maximum of seven. Within the 16 settings with E off, each eight-run experiment is one parity condition on A through D. To avoid both omitted settings, the parity must agree on them and we choose the opposite value. Seven nonempty subsets of the four switches have even size, giving seven such conditions.

Schedule II leaves three settings missing from the E-off group. To exclude all three, a nonempty subset must have even size and contain either both C and D or neither. Exactly three qualify: AB, CD and ABCD. The single E-on setting cannot complete another experiment, since any affine cube on which E varies has four settings of each kind. Schedule II therefore preserves three experiments.
two-missing-lamps.limitation: A count of complete experiments measures this particular design objective. Schedule I never turns E on, so a fault that occurs only with E on can escape all fourteen tests.
two-missing-lamps.investigate: List both schedules in a spreadsheet and model a warning that appears exactly when E is on and A is off. Run both lists and count the warnings. Compare that observation with the seven-versus-three prediction, then choose a schedule for a lab whose priority is finding that warning.
